newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Malaysia telecoms early equal access unlikely.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Malaysia telecoms early equal access unlikely.

text.p: The advent of equal access in the telecommunications industry for Malaysian subscribers is unlikely to be brought forward, said analysts on Monday.

Equal access implies that all of state telecommunications firm Telekom Malaysia Bhd's three million subscribers would be able to use alternative trunk and international networks offered by its Malaysian competitors. Under a current agreement between industry players equal access would be introduced on January 1, 1999.

"Two years is not a long time. It might not happen sooner. Other operators (apart from Telekom Malaysia) would lobby for it, but it is questionable whether they would be ready for it," said Soon Teck Onn, telecommunications analyst at equities research house ING-Barings in Kuala Lumpur.
On Monday, Malaysian Energy, Telecommunications and Posts Minister Leo Moggie hinted that he would welcome the early advent of equal access.
"We are committed to implementing equal access by January 1, 1999. But if we can bring it forward, so much the better," Moggie told reporters after opening an electronics conference.
"If we delay the implementation then we are maintaining a monopoly," Moggie added.
Telekom stock has recently come under pressure on speculation that competition within the industry would squeeze margins, including the earlier start of the equal access agreements.
The stock on Monday ended down 60 cents or 2.8 percent to 20.60 ringgit.
Telekom's chief executive, Mohamed Said Mohamed Ali, said on Monday that he was committed to commencing equal access on January 1, 1999, and would have to refer to Moggie on any change.
But analysts said the implementation of equal access would involve lengthy negotiations between the country's seven licence holders of fixed-line services.

"They would have to agree on inter-connectivity, the universal service agreement, a formula for pricing and the inherited cost base," said a telecommunnications analyst at a foreign brokerage house in Kuala Lumpur.

Inter-connectivity refers to the agreements between the various service providers for subscribers to use each other's systems. The universal service agreement would force smaller telecommunication companies to provide services to unprofitable rural areas, while the inherited cost base refers to the use of Telekom Malaysia's existing land lines.

"Telekom would probably have to lower its prices, and its earnings growth would certainly slow down," said Soon. "Nobody really knows the impact on Telekom if equal access is brought forward, but it would certainly be negative".
